client: I've been really struggling since I graduated back in May. I can't seem to land a job in my field no matter how many applications I send out, and watching my friends and classmates move into their careers while I'm still stuck just makes me feel like there's something fundamentally wrong with me. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It means a lot that you took this step, even through the doubt — that takes real courage. What you're feeling makes complete sense; the gap between where you hoped to be and where you are right now is genuinely painful, and comparing your journey to others' can make it feel so much more isolating. I'm curious, though — when you say there's "something fundamentally wrong" with you, what does that inner voice sound like, and where do you think it's drawing that conclusion from?

client: That voice... it's pretty harsh, honestly. It says things like "everyone else figured out how to make real friends and build a life by now, so if you haven't, it must mean you're just broken in some way that can't be fixed." I think it draws from years of feeling like I'm always on the outside of things, watching other people connect easily while I'm standing there not knowing what to say or do.
therapist: That voice is incredibly harsh, and I want you to notice something — it's taking a very real and painful experience (feeling on the outside) and leaping to a permanent, sweeping conclusion about who you *are* as a person, rather than reflecting a situation you've been navigating. That feeling of watching others connect easily while you struggle is something so many people carry quietly, and it doesn't mean you're broken — it might mean connection has felt harder or less safe for you, which is something that can genuinely shift. What do you think that "outside" feeling has looked like across your life — has it been there in every situation, or are there moments where it's felt a little less present?

client: I guess it hasn't always been there at the same intensity... like, when I'm with my sister, sometimes it feels a little easier, less like I'm performing. But even then, there's this background hum of waiting for the moment when she'll realize I'm not as interesting or worthwhile as she thinks I am. So I don't know if that really counts as a moment where it's less present, or if it's just a quieter version of the same thing.
therapist: What you just described actually tells us something really important — there *is* a version of connection that feels more natural for you, even if it's accompanied by that quiet fear of being "found out." That fear of being unmasked, of someone eventually seeing through you, is so common it even has a name in CBT circles — it's often called the "waiting for the other shoe to drop" pattern, and it can rob us of fully inhabiting the moments of genuine warmth that are already there. I'm wondering — when you're with your sister and it feels easier, what do you think is different about that space that allows even a little bit of that guard to come down?

client: I think with my sister it's partly because she already knows the worst versions of me — she's seen me fall apart before and she didn't leave. But even saying that out loud makes me nervous, like I'm jinxing it somehow, or like I'm admitting there's something to be "found out" in the first place. I'm not sure I fully trust that the ease I feel with her is real, or if I'm just... less guarded because I've given up on impressing her.
therapist: What you just said is actually quite profound — that being truly known, including the messy parts, created *more* safety rather than less, which is the opposite of what that harsh inner voice predicts will happen when people "find out" who you are. And I want to gently push back on the idea that feeling less guarded because you've "given up impressing her" is somehow lesser — that might actually be the closest thing to real intimacy, where you're just *you* without the performance. What do you think it would mean for you if that ease turned out to be genuinely real, rather than just a lowered defense?

client: I mean... if it were genuinely real, that would be kind of terrifying, honestly. Because then I'd have to accept that maybe I've been wrong this whole time about needing to keep people at a distance to stay safe. And I don't know if I'm ready to let go of that belief, even if part of me wants to.
therapist: That kind of honesty — recognizing that a belief might be protecting you *and* limiting you at the same time — is really the heart of so much of the work we do here, and it takes real self-awareness to see it so clearly. It makes complete sense that you'd feel reluctant to release something that has felt like a shield, even if it's also been keeping warmth out. I'm curious — if you didn't have to let go of that belief all at once, but just got to gently *question* it in small moments, what might that look like for you?

client: I guess... maybe it could look like noticing when I automatically assume someone doesn't really want me around, and just pausing for a second instead of immediately pulling back. But honestly, even imagining that feels kind of exposing, like I'd be leaving myself open to getting hurt. I'm not sure I trust that the pause would lead anywhere good rather than just confirming what I already believe.
therapist: That instinct to pause rather than immediately retreat is actually a really meaningful shift, and the fact that you could even imagine it tells me something important about your readiness, even if it doesn't feel that way yet. The fear that the pause will just confirm your worst beliefs is so understandable — but I want you to notice that right now, in this conversation, you've paused and stayed open rather than pulling back, and something real has emerged from that. What do you think you've actually found out about yourself today that you didn't expect to?

client: I guess... I didn't expect to find out that I could actually sit with something uncomfortable without completely shutting down. That's kind of surprising to me, because usually the moment things start feeling too real in a conversation, I just go quiet or change the subject. I'm not sure what to do with that information yet, but I'll admit it doesn't feel totally worthless to notice it.
therapist: That right there — "it doesn't feel totally worthless to notice it" — might be one of the most honest and hopeful things you've said today, and I don't want it to slip by unacknowledged, because you just did something your inner voice told you wasn't possible. You stayed, you went toward the uncomfortable thing instead of away from it, and you came out the other side with something new about yourself rather than confirmation of your fears. I'm wondering — how does it feel to sit with that, even just for a moment, without immediately explaining it away?

client: I mean... it feels kind of strange, honestly. Like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop, or for myself to realize I'm making too big a deal out of something small. But I guess there's also this tiny quiet part of me that's like... okay, maybe that actually did mean something.
therapist: That tiny quiet part deserves just as much of your attention as the loud voice that's quick to minimize — and I want you to notice that you didn't dismiss it entirely this time, you let it speak even if just for a moment. The "waiting for the other shoe to drop" feeling makes complete sense given everything you've carried, but today you've actually gathered a small piece of real evidence that contradicts the story of being broken and unreachable. I'm curious — what might it look like to be just a little bit loyal to that quiet part this week, even in one small moment?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to hold onto that... but I honestly don't know what "being loyal to that quiet part" even looks like in practice. Like, when I'm alone in my apartment and the anxiety kicks in, that loud voice is so much faster and stronger — it's hard to imagine the quieter one having any real chance. I guess I'm worried that if I try to nurture it and it doesn't work, I'll just feel more broken than before.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — it feels safer not to try than to try and have it confirm your worst fears, and that's actually a really common way we protect ourselves when we've been hurt by hope before. But I want to offer a small reframe: being loyal to that quiet part doesn't have to mean nurturing it into something strong enough to win against the loud voice — it could be as small as just *noticing* when it shows up, the way you did just now, without immediately letting the loud voice talk you out of it. What if the goal this week wasn't to silence the harsh voice, but just to catch one moment where the quieter one surfaces and simply say to yourself, "there it is" — do you think that might feel manageable?

client: I mean... maybe. It sounds simple enough in theory, but I guess my worry is that even noticing it will just set off the loud voice faster, like I'm poking a beehive just by paying attention. I don't know if I trust that "there it is" will feel like enough — part of me thinks I'll just end up feeling worse for having noticed something I can't do anything with.
therapist: That worry is really worth taking seriously — you're not being resistant, you're being honest about how your inner world actually works, and that's valuable information rather than a problem to fix. What I'd gently offer is that you've already poked that beehive today, several times, and the loud voice came up *and* the quiet one still managed to say something worth hearing — so you've already run a small version of this experiment right here. I'm wondering, looking back at this conversation, whether the act of noticing actually made things worse, or whether something else happened that you didn't quite predict?
